blocks.text: Reproduction Annelids can reproduce both sexually and asexually. Most annelids have separate sexes, but some, such as earthworms and leeches, are hermaphrodites. Sperm are passed between two worms near segments called the clitellum. Refer back to Figure 25.23 and notice that the clitellum is a thickened band of segments. It produces a cocoon from which young earthworms hatch, as shown in Figure 25.26. Sperm and eggs pass into the cocoon as it slips forward off the body of the worm. After fertilization, the young are protected in the cocoon as they develop. Some annelids reproduce asexually by fragmentation. If a worm breaks apart, the missing parts can be regenerated.

blocks.text: The phylum Annelida is divided into three classes: class Oligochaeta (ohl ih goh KEE tuh)—the earthworms and their relatives, class Polychaeta (pah lih KEE tuh)—the bristleworms and their relatives, and class Hirudinea (hur uh DIN ee uh)—the leeches.

Earthworms and their relatives Earthworms probably are the best-known annelids. They are used as bait for fishing and are found in garden soil. An earthworm can eat its own mass in soil every day. Earthworms ingest soil to extract nutrients. In this way, earthworms aerate the soil—they break up the soil to allow air and water to move through it.
blocks.features: 'Earthworms and their relatives' is a bold brownish-red run-in heading.

blocks.text: In addition to earthworms, class Oligochaeta—the oligochaetes (AH lee goh keetz)—includes tubifex worms and lumbriculid worms. Tubifex worms are small, threadlike aquatic annelids that are common in areas of high pollution. Lumbriculid (lum BRIH kyuh lid) worms are freshwater oligochaetes that are about 6 cm long and live at the edges of lakes and ponds. You can observe a feature common to oligochaetes in MiniLab 25.2.

blocks.text: Observe Blood Flow in a Segmented Worm
blocks.features: Dark blue text on a light blue gradient banner.

blocks.text: How does blood flow in a segmented worm? The California blackworm has a closed circulatory system and a transparent body. Its blood can be viewed as it flows along the dorsal blood vessel.

blocks.features: Bold dark blue text, accompanied by four small safety icons.

items.text: Read and complete the lab safety form.
Moisten a piece of filter paper with spring water and place it in a Petri dish.
Examine a blackworm on the moist paper using a stereomicroscope.
Locate the dorsal blood vessel in a segment near the midpoint of the worm. Observe how blood flows in each segment.
Use a stopwatch to record how many pulses of blood occur per minute. Repeat this for two more segments, one near the head and one near the tail of the worm. Record your data in a table.

blocks.features: Numbered list; the first word of each item is bold.

items.text: Summarize how blood moves through each segment, including the direction of blood flow.
Compare and contrast the rate of blood flow near the head, at the midpoint, and near the tail of the worm.
